title: 27.4 A BJT-Based Temperature Sensor with an 80fJ.K2 Resolution FoM
problem: BJT-based temperature sensors require high energy efficiency while maintaining high accuracy; existing designs using resistor-based sensors or CT-ΔΣM approaches consume more power or occupy larger area.
motivation: On-chip temperature sensing for thermal management in high-performance chips demands both excellent energy efficiency (fJ.K^2 scale) and high accuracy without significant area overhead; prior BJT sensors lag resistor designs in energy efficiency.
method: The sensor uses an NPN transistor—a type of semiconductor—to generate two currents that change with temperature: one increasing (PTAT, proportional to absolute temperature) and one decreasing (CTAT, complementary to absolute temperature). A continuous-time delta-sigma modulator digitizes the ratio of these currents, converting analog signals to digital form for precise temperature measurement. A current-assisted amplifier strengthens this ratio without adding noise, reducing the energy needed for accurate conversion.
key_novelty: By combining charge-balancing in the delta-sigma modulator (which keeps charge flow stable to reduce noise) with a current-assisted amplifier, the sensor uses 2.5 times less energy than previous designs.
contributions: 80fJ.K^2 FoM—2.5x more energy efficient than prior work
Compact 0.05mm^2 area—1.5x smaller than prior designs
BJT-based approach competitive with resistor-based sensors in energy efficiency
baselines: Prior BJT sensors with charge-balancing CTΔΣM
Conventional BJT sensors with discrete time quantizers
limitations: Focuses on BJT design; comparison with resistor-based sensors primarily on energy; dynamic range and supply-voltage variation effects not detailed.
primary_theme: Energy-efficient BJT temperature sensor via noise-optimized CTΔΣM
